subtitle: Qwen3.8-27B at four precisions, each on a single RTX PRO 6000, three decision models, and an observer guidance prompt, all called through a LiteLLM gateway and scored on frames from Sycan Marsh ("Sycan") and Hanna Hammock ("Florida").
summary: We tested which model should run the recon gateway's planning, image checks and writeup, whether a dedicated decision model (Kai 0.6B, Clef-Flash 9B or Clef 27B) should make the fire call instead of the LLM, and whether a generic observer guidance prompt helps models notice fire. Every call went through one LiteLLM gateway with fixed sampling, validated tool calls and logged runs; 600 full briefs and more than 8,000 single-frame checks completed with no failures. With thermal data every Qwen3.8-27B precision gets fire status right. The hard case is small fires seen in RGB only, where most models say no fire. The guidance prompt, written once and never tuned, raised single-frame recall on two separate frame samples for every Qwen3.8 build (FP8 only slightly) and for both Clef models, with no new false alarms. The measurement rule using guided BF16 image checks found 4 of 7 small RGB fires, against at most 1 for any model's own call.
stats: Full briefs completed through the gateway, with no failed or unfinished tool-calling runs
Single-frame answers that changed when the same check was run again
Recall gain from the observer guidance on the second frame sample (Qwen3.8 BF16, 0.38 to 0.48), with no added false alarms
Sequences right with the measurement rule on guided BF16 image checks, against 14 for the best LLM writeup call
FP8 decoding speed over BF16, with the same writeup accuracy
recommendations: Run the gateway LLM as Qwen3.8-27B, one build per RTX PRO 6000. Use BF16 with the observer guidance when image judgments matter most: guided BF16 has the best single-frame recall (0.53 and 0.48 on the two samples, against 0.43 and 0.42 for guided FP8), and the measurement rule on its image checks found 4 of 7 small RGB fires, against 2 of 7 with guided FP8. Use FP8 when speed matters: its writeup call is as accurate (42 of 60 briefs), it decodes 1.7 times faster and a brief takes 30 s instead of 43 s. Avoid INT4 for image judgments.

Keep the observer guidance on the per-frame image checks, where it raised recall on new frames with no false alarms. With the guidance on in the planner, image checks and writeup at once, the writeup's own call did not improve (BF16 fell from 42 to 39 of 60). Leave it out of the planner and writeup until a run with guidance on the image checks only confirms that split.

Keep thermal as the authority whenever a frame has it. For RGB-only footage, the measurement rule on three guided BF16 image checks found 4 of 7 small-fire sequences with no false alarms, against at most 1 for any model's own call (on guided FP8 or NVFP4 checks it found 2 of 7, and on INT4 none). Test it on more no-fire RGB footage before letting it override the writeup.

Do not make Kai, Clef or Clef-Flash the fire-status decider. From the measurements alone none of them caught a small RGB fire, and given the unguided BF16 image checks only Clef-Flash caught 1 of 7. Kai answers in about 0.1 s, so it may suit fast sub-questions such as confidence, but this report did not test that.
Small fires in RGB-only footage are the open gap. Add small, under-canopy fires like Florida plot 2 to the detector's training data, as the mentor suggested.
tk_setup: Five LLM routes (Qwen3.8-27B in BF16, FP8, INT4 and NVFP4, plus the earlier Qwen3-VL-4B), three decision models, 20 test sequences scored three times each, and two separate samples of single frames.
setup:
LLM routes. Qwen3.8-27B is a 27-billion-parameter model that reads images and text. A model's precision is how many bits store each number in it. Fewer bits (quantization) make the model smaller and faster but can cost accuracy. BF16 is the original 16-bit model (about 56 GB), FP8 the official 8-bit version (about 31 GB), INT4 stores weights in 4 bits but computes in 16 bits, and NVFP4 stores weights and activations in a 4-bit format the RTX PRO 6000 supports in hardware (about 26 GB). Each ran on its own RTX PRO 6000 with the same serving software (vLLM v0.31.0) and settings, except that BF16 also caps concurrent requests at 256 to fit in memory. The model's built-in step-by-step reasoning mode was off. The earlier gateway model, Qwen3-VL-4B on a smaller L4 GPU, is the baseline.

Decision models. Kai 0.6B reads text only. Clef 27B and Clef-Flash 9B read text plus images. All three answer fixed multiple-choice questions (fire, smoke only, none, unclear) with a probability for each option instead of writing text.

Test material. Twenty sequences of eight frames, scored three times each: 8 with thermal and 12 with RGB only, including 7 windows of small fires that the RGB detector misses. Florida fire truth comes from the thermal camera (any pixel at 80 C or above); pre-burn flights count as no fire because they were flown before ignition; Sycan truth comes from the dataset's fire and no-fire labels. Single-frame checks used 240 frames: Florida 40 large-fire, 40 small-fire, 60 pre-burn and 20 during-burn frames with no hot pixel, plus 40 Sycan fire and 40 Sycan no-fire frames. A second sample of 221 frames shares none of them; only 1 unused during-burn frame with no hot pixel was left for it.
tk_gateway: Every model call went through one LiteLLM gateway, and the tool-calling loop was rebuilt after two code reviews. Repeating a run almost always gave the same answer, invalid tool calls are rejected, and models see neutral ids instead of names that hint at the answer.
gateway:
The gateway exposes one OpenAI-compatible endpoint for the five LLM routes and pass-through routes for the fire classifier, Kai, Clef and Clef-Flash. It logs every request with a run tag, its latency, token counts, finish reason and tool-call names. An unsupported request parameter is an error rather than being dropped silently.

Two code reviews of the gateway, with each reported problem confirmed by a second check before it was fixed, led to these changes before the final runs:

  • Answer scoring. A bug counted a whitespace token as the answer letter for "yes", which turned some fire answers into "no" and hit NVFP4 hardest. Fixing it raised NVFP4's single-frame ROC AUC (the ranking score explained below) from 0.78 to 0.90. INT4, FP8 and BF16 moved by 0.02 or less.
  • No hidden answers. Sequence and frame names such as "smallfire" or "preburn" reached the model in the first version. Models now see neutral ids (f01 to f08).
  • Fixed sampling. Temperature 0 and a fixed seed on every call, and one request at a time per model for scored single-frame checks.
  • Measurements first. The gateway runs the detector, thermal tools, spread tracking and three fixed image checks itself. The planner can only choose up to three more frames to check, with tool calls forced, frame ids limited to the real ones and every argument validated.
  • Strict output. The writeup must match a JSON schema, evidence is sent complete and in a fixed order, and the measured hot-area percentage is filled in by code instead of the model.
  • The measurement rule. This is code, not a model. With thermal, it calls fire when the thermal frames show a pixel at 80 C or above. Without thermal, it calls fire when the detector flags at least half the frames, or when at least 2 of the 3 fixed image checks (first, middle and last frame) say flames are visible with a yes-probability of 0.8 or more. Otherwise it calls no fire. Thermal data, or a detector that flags most frames, can overrule the LLM's writeup; weaker RGB-only evidence is recorded as a note instead.
tk_frames: On single frames, the Qwen3.8 builds rank fire frames well but answer "no" unless they see flames clearly. BF16 and FP8 judge best, INT4 and NVFP4 lose some, and no model raised a false alarm.
frames_intro: Each model got one RGB frame and the question "Are flames or glowing fire visible in this aerial image?" Recall is the share of fire frames the model answered yes to. ROC AUC measures how well the model's yes-probability ranks fire frames above no-fire frames, where 1.0 is a perfect ranking and 0.5 is chance. Large fires cover at least 0.5% of the thermal view at 80 C or more and small fires cover less, with 40 frames in each Florida fire group.
r_frames0: BF16 (recall 0.40, AUC 0.94) and FP8 (0.43, 0.93) are the strongest Qwen3.8 builds. NVFP4 (0.37, 0.90) and INT4 (0.21, 0.90) lose ground, INT4 mostly on small fires. Clef and Clef-Flash rank well (AUC about 0.97) but say yes less often. The old Qwen3-VL-4B shows an even higher AUC (0.975), but only because it ranks frames by vanishingly small yes-probabilities: it says yes on just 15% of fire frames, and on its rounded probabilities its AUC is 0.68. Running the whole check again changed none of the 1,680 answers.
r_frames1: The second sample repeats the pattern: BF16 0.38 and FP8 0.40 recall, NVFP4 0.32, INT4 0.20, with no false alarms on 101 negatives.
tk_guidance: The observer guidance raised single-frame recall for every Qwen3.8 build (FP8 only slightly), and for both Clef models, on both samples, with no new false alarms. In full briefs it did not help the Qwen3.8 writeups' own call (BF16 fell from 42 to 39 of 60); only the old 4B improved, from 33 to 36.
guidance_intro: The guidance is a short text, given to each LLM as a system message and appended to the question for Clef and Clef-Flash, describing what an aerial fire observer watches for (flame and glow, embers, burn edges, smoke rising from a source) and common look-alikes (bare soil, sun glint, haze, old burn scars). It was written once from general fire-observation practice, with no values from these two burns, and was not changed after seeing results. The second sample shares no frames with the first.
r_guidance: On the second sample the gain was +0.10 for BF16, +0.11 for NVFP4, +0.07 for INT4, +0.02 for FP8, +0.18 for Clef and +0.07 for Clef-Flash, with zero false alarms throughout. In the briefs, the 300 guided runs turned on the guidance in the planner, image checks and writeup together. There the writeup's own call did not improve for any Qwen3.8 build (BF16 42 to 39 of 60 correct, FP8 42 to 42, NVFP4 42 to 41, INT4 39 to 39); only the 4B baseline rose, 33 to 36. The measurement rule using guided BF16 image checks rose from 45 to 51 of 60.
tk_briefs: With thermal data, every Qwen3.8 build is right on every brief. With RGB only, all of them are right on the no-fire and large-fire sequences, and nearly all miss the small fires. Repeated runs gave the same answer on 199 of 200 route and sequence pairs.
briefs_intro: Each brief runs the full gateway: measurements, three fixed image checks, the planner's extra checks, then the writeup. The table scores the writeup's own fire call before any policy correction, over 20 sequences times 3 repeats. The small-fire and no-fire columns count sequences by the majority of the three repeats.
r_briefs: All four Qwen3.8 builds were right on all 24 thermal briefs and on every RGB-only no-fire sequence. Without guidance, BF16, FP8 and NVFP4 each caught one of the 7 RGB-only small-fire sequences and INT4 caught none; with guidance, BF16 caught none. The earlier Qwen3-VL-4B also missed a thermal small-fire sequence and called the Sycan fire SY-2_5 smoke only.
r_planner: Across 600 briefs, no plan went unfinished and no response was cut off by the token limit. The gateway rejected and explained 8 invalid tool calls, all on INT4 and NVFP4 with guidance. The 4B model spent about a third of its extra checks re-asking a question the gateway had already asked on the same frame. FP8 and NVFP4 finished a brief in about 25 to 30 seconds, BF16 in about 43.
tk_deciders: The measurement rule was the most accurate fire call: 17 of 20 sequences on guided BF16 image checks and 15 of 20 on unguided ones, against 14 for the best Qwen3.8 writeup. The three decision models scored 11 to 13, mainly because they missed the small RGB fires.
deciders_intro: Kai, Clef and Clef-Flash got the same measurements in words: detector results, a general image classifier's results, thermal results and camera motion. Clef and Clef-Flash also saw the first and last frames. A second pass also gave them the three fixed image checks from the unguided BF16 run (first repeat), so all three read identical evidence. On those same unguided checks the measurement rule scored 15 of 20, with 2 of 7 small fires. The decision models were not tested with the guided checks.
r_deciders: Without the image checks, Clef-Flash got 13 of 20, Kai 12 and Clef 11. With them, all three scored 12: Kai did not change, Clef fixed the thermal small fire FL-B, and Clef-Flash caught one small RGB fire (FL-G) but called two thermal fire sequences (FL-C and SY-2_5) smoke only. The decision models are fast (Kai about 0.1 s per call) but read the evidence more conservatively than the LLM does.
tk_speed: Lower precision buys speed: FP8 decodes 1.7 times faster than BF16, NVFP4 2 times, INT4 2.8 times. Every Qwen3.8 build fits on one RTX PRO 6000.
r_speed: Measured on a text-only prompt with 384 output tokens, one request decodes at 26 tokens per second on BF16, 45 on FP8, 52 on NVFP4 and 74 on INT4. With 8 requests at once the totals are 197, 317, 357 and 485. A whole brief took a median of 43 seconds on BF16, 30 on FP8, 25 on NVFP4 and 26 on INT4.
method_notes: Fire truth for the Florida burn sequences comes from the thermal camera (any pixel at 80 C or above), and on thermal sequences the gateway also uses that signal, so those results show the pipeline works rather than testing vision. Pre-burn sequences count as no fire because they were flown before ignition and have no thermal frames.

The brief comparison of precisions comes down to the 7 RGB-only small-fire sequences; on the other 13, every Qwen3.8 build is right. Read small differences there with care. FL-G is the same 8 frames as FL-B with thermal withheld.
The guided brief arm turned the guidance on in three places at once. The single-frame test isolates the image-check placement and is the cleaner evidence.

The image-check part of the measurement rule was tested for false alarms on only 4 RGB-only no-fire sequences (FL-D, FL-N, FL-O, FL-P). On the two thermal no-fire sequences (FL-E and SY-2_7), thermal decides. The rule needs more no-fire RGB footage before it should overrule a writeup.
Clef and Clef-Flash ran on their reference Python code, which is slower than an optimized server, so their timings are upper bounds.
Single-frame checks sent one request at a time per model, with temperature 0 and a fixed seed, so a rerun reproduced every answer. Batching requests on a server can shift answers slightly.

Sequences FL-H to FL-P were added after a review found that only one sequence separated the models. They were chosen by frame number: the small-fire ones from the thermal-labeled plot 2 small-fire range, and the no-fire ones from the pre-burn flights. None were chosen from model results.
prompt_intro: The full text, used unchanged in every guided run. It contains nothing specific to the two test burns.
